prompt: A login form pastes the typed username straight into its SQL query. An attacker types ' OR '1'='1 as the username. What is the main risk?
options: The attacker may bypass the login by altering the query
The website will run out of storage
The user's browser will stop working
The password will be encrypted twice
correct: The attacker may bypass the login by altering the query

prompt: A comment box shows whatever visitors type as live HTML. An attacker posts a script tag. What happens when other visitors open the page?
options: The server's disk is wiped immediately
The script runs in their browsers and may steal session data
Their passwords are reset automatically
Nothing, because browsers ignore scripts in comments
correct: The script runs in their browsers and may steal session data

prompt: Which backup approach best follows the 3-2-1 rule?
options: Three copies, on two different media types, with one copy kept off-site
One copy on a USB drive kept at the desk
Two copies, both on the office network
Three copies stored in different folders on the same server
correct: Three copies, on two different media types, with one copy kept off-site

prompt: Why is a password manager safer than reusing one strong password on many sites?
options: It removes the need for any login at all
It stores passwords in the browser history
A breach at one site cannot unlock the user's other accounts
It makes passwords shorter and easier to remember
correct: A breach at one site cannot unlock the user's other accounts

prompt: Which statement about asymmetric encryption is correct?
options: It uses a single shared secret key for both sides
It can only be used when offline
It uses a public key and a private key as a pair
It needs no keys at all
correct: It uses a public key and a private key as a pair

prompt: Why are stored passwords hashed instead of simply encrypted?
options: Hashed passwords never need to be unique
Hashes make logins faster for the user
Hashing lets administrators read forgotten passwords
A hash cannot be reversed to read the original, so a stolen database reveals less
correct: A hash cannot be reversed to read the original, so a stolen database reveals less

prompt: A website shows a padlock in the address bar. What does this tell you for certain?
options: The site is run by a trustworthy company
The connection between you and the site is encrypted
The site is free of malware
The site cannot be a phishing site
correct: The connection between you and the site is encrypted

prompt: A shop's website goes down after millions of requests per second arrive from thousands of infected devices. What is this attack?
options: SQL injection
Credential stuffing
Man-in-the-middle
Distributed denial of service (DDoS)
correct: Distributed denial of service (DDoS)

prompt: Attackers try email and password pairs leaked from one breached site on many other sites. What is this called?
options: Clickjacking
Session fixation
Cross-site scripting
Credential stuffing
correct: Credential stuffing

prompt: Finance receives an email that appears to come from the CEO, asking for an urgent transfer to a new bank account and to tell no one. What is the best first action?
options: Forward it to colleagues and wait for opinions
Verify the request through a separate known channel, such as phoning the CEO
Reply to the email asking for the account details again
Make the transfer quickly because the CEO is senior
correct: Verify the request through a separate known channel, such as phoning the CEO

prompt: A caller claiming to be from your bank asks for the OTP you just received by SMS, saying it will cancel a fraud transaction. What should you do?
options: Hang up, never share the OTP, and call the bank's official number
Share only the last three digits
Read out the OTP quickly to stop the fraud
Ask the caller to call back after you share it by email
correct: Hang up, never share the OTP, and call the bank's official number

prompt: Which is the safest way to do work on a cafe's public Wi-Fi?
options: Use any open network with the same name as the cafe
Connect through the company VPN
Disable the device firewall so pages load faster
Turn off the screen lock for speed
correct: Connect through the company VPN

prompt: Which statement best describes zero trust?
options: Trust users for a year after they log in once
Never trust by default; verify every user and device for each access request
Trust everyone who is inside the office network
Trust any device that has antivirus installed
correct: Never trust by default; verify every user and device for each access request

prompt: Why do organizations keep guest Wi-Fi separate from the internal network?
options: So guest traffic is never logged
So the internal network needs no passwords
So guests get faster internet
So a compromised guest device cannot reach internal systems directly
correct: So a compromised guest device cannot reach internal systems directly

prompt: Which tool continuously watches laptops and servers for suspicious behaviour and can isolate an infected device?
options: A network printer
Endpoint detection and response (EDR)
A DNS server
A password policy
correct: Endpoint detection and response (EDR)

prompt: A decoy system is deliberately set up to attract attackers so their methods can be studied. What is it called?
options: A backup server
A honeypot
A firewall
A proxy
correct: A honeypot

prompt: A vulnerability scores 9.8 on CVSS and can be exploited from the internet with no login. How should it be treated?
options: As low priority, since scores are only advisory
As something to ignore until users complain
As critical, to be patched or mitigated urgently
As something to review at the next yearly audit
correct: As critical, to be patched or mitigated urgently

prompt: Which email controls help stop attackers from spoofing your company's domain?
options: Shorter email signatures
Dark mode in the email client
Larger mailbox quotas
SPF, DKIM and DMARC
correct: SPF, DKIM and DMARC

prompt: A hospital's patient records are quietly altered by an attacker. Which part of the CIA triad is mainly lost?
options: Portability
Integrity
Confidentiality
Availability
correct: Integrity

prompt: Why does chain of custody matter for digital evidence?
options: It makes the evidence load faster
It allows anyone to edit the original
It deletes sensitive data after analysis
It records who handled the evidence and when, so it stays trustworthy
correct: It records who handled the evidence and when, so it stays trustworthy

prompt: Which incident deserves the highest severity rating?
options: A user forgetting their password
A spam email blocked by the filter
Ransomware encrypting the main customer database
A single failed login attempt
correct: Ransomware encrypting the main customer database

prompt: An employee who has just resigned copies thousands of customer files to a personal drive. Which risk is this?
options: Insider threat and data exfiltration
A denial of service attack
A routine software update
A harmless backup
correct: Insider threat and data exfiltration

prompt: Staff begin using an unapproved file-sharing app to send client data. What is this called?
options: Zero trust
Patch management
Shadow IT
Penetration testing
correct: Shadow IT

prompt: Which pair counts as true multi-factor authentication?
options: A PIN and a password
A password and a fingerprint
A password and a security question
Two different passwords
correct: A password and a fingerprint

prompt: An attacker alters DNS records so people typing your bank's address land on a fake copy. What is this called?
options: Keylogging
DNS spoofing (cache poisoning)
Port scanning
Tailgating
correct: DNS spoofing (cache poisoning)

prompt: What is the main purpose of a SIEM?
options: Print security reports on paper
Speed up the internet connection
Collect and correlate logs from many systems to detect threats
Store employee passwords
correct: Collect and correlate logs from many systems to detect threats

prompt: What makes recovery from ransomware most reliable?
options: Deleting all logs
Clean, tested, offline backups
Rebooting every machine
Paying the ransom quickly
correct: Clean, tested, offline backups

prompt: How does a penetration test differ from a vulnerability scan?
options: A scan exploits weaknesses and a pen test does not
A pen test is fully automated and a scan is manual
They are exactly the same thing
A pen test tries to exploit weaknesses, while a scan only identifies them
correct: A pen test tries to exploit weaknesses, while a scan only identifies them

prompt: In MITRE ATT&CK, what do tactics describe?
options: The brand of malware used
The location of the attacker
The attacker's goals at each stage, such as persistence or exfiltration
The age of the vulnerability
correct: The attacker's goals at each stage, such as persistence or exfiltration

scenario: A staff member leaves a laptop in a parked car overnight. The laptop has no disk encryption and holds customer records.
flags: The laptop has no disk encryption
It was left unattended in a car
The laptop is company property
Customer records are stored digitally
correctFlags: The laptop has no disk encryption
It was left unattended in a car

scenario: A developer commits a file containing a database password to a public code repository, then deletes the file in the next commit.
flags: A secret was published in a public repository
Deleting it later is assumed to remove it from history
The developer uses version control
The file was inside a repository
correctFlags: A secret was published in a public repository
Deleting it later is assumed to remove it from history

scenario: A hospital's Wi-Fi uses one shared password that has not changed in five years and is known to all former staff.
flags: The password is shared by everyone
It has not been changed in five years
Former staff still know it
The hospital offers Wi-Fi
correctFlags: The password is shared by everyone
It has not been changed in five years

scenario: A user gets an email from support@paypa1-help.com saying the account closes in 2 hours unless they click a link and enter their login.
flags: The sender domain imitates the real brand
The message creates artificial urgency
It asks for a login through a link
The email mentions a company name
correctFlags: The sender domain imitates the real brand
It asks for a login through a link

scenario: An admin turns off the server firewall 'temporarily' to troubleshoot and forgets to turn it back on for three months.
flags: The firewall was left disabled
No one tracked the temporary change
Troubleshooting was needed
The server is in a data centre
correctFlags: No one tracked the temporary change

scenario: A company lets every employee install any software and run as local administrator on their laptop.
flags: Everyone has local administrator rights
Unrestricted software installation is allowed
Employees use laptops
The company has employees

scenario: A receptionist holds the door for a delivery person in an unfamiliar uniform who says he left his badge in the van.
flags: No identity or authorization check was made
Courtesy replaced the visitor procedure
The visitor wore a uniform
The door is a main entrance
correctFlags: No identity or authorization check was made

scenario: A team keeps its only backup on a drive permanently plugged into the same server it protects.
flags: The only backup sits on the same server
The backup is always connected, so ransomware can encrypt it too
Backups are being taken
The backup uses a drive
correctFlags: The only backup sits on the same server
The backup is always connected, so ransomware can encrypt it too

prompt: Arrange the steps for handling a suspected phishing email from the employee's side.
steps: Do not click or open anything
Report it to the security team
Security analyses and blocks the sender

prompt: Arrange the stages of a secure software development lifecycle.
Arrange the steps of securely onboarding a new employee.
steps: Create an account with least privilege

prompt: Arrange the steps of a safe helpdesk password reset.
steps: Send it through a separate channel
Force a change at next login

prompt: Arrange the steps of handling digital evidence.
Arrange the steps of a risk assessment.
steps: Decide how to treat each risk

pairs.definition: Floods a service until it is unavailable
Inserts malicious commands through input fields
Identifies that an incident has occurred
A public and private key pair
Attaches to files and spreads when they run
